content: Subsequent trials confirmed its efficacy among heterosexual men and women. Between January and March 2011, participants in an ongoing phase 2b HIV vaccine efficacy trial completed an anonymous web survey about PrEP. Among 376 respondents, 17% reported being very likely to use PrEP within the next year, with nonwhite participants showing a higher likelihood of interest. Those interested in PrEP were most inclined to use it if it were available through clinical trials or covered by health insurance. Most participants (91%) believed that taking PrEP would not affect their willingness to remain in the vaccine trial, nor did they think it would impact recruitment efforts. Current trial participants, as key stakeholders, can provide valuable insights into emerging prevention technologies that may influence the design of future HIV vaccine and non-vaccine prevention trials. A 2011 study by Galea et al. explored the acceptability of PrEP among at-risk populations in Lima, Peru, including female sex workers, transgender individuals, and MSM. Focus groups identified social issues affecting PrEP acceptability, while conjoint analysis evaluated preferences across eight hypothetical PrEP scenarios. Findings highlighted concerns about sexual risk disinhibition, stigma, discrimination, and mistrust of healthcare professionals, which require careful consideration during PrEP rollout planning. In 2012, Galindo et al. examined community perspectives on PrEP among transgender women and MSM in California. Semi-structured interviews with 30 participants revealed limited community awareness and confusion about PrEP, as well as concerns about equity and how PrEP interventions would be marketed. Effective PrEP implementation must address these concerns to reduce HIV health disparities. A 2013 study by Gilmore et al. investigated the experiences of iPrEx trial participants in San Francisco, where adherence to PrEP was high. Participants joined the study out of altruism, valued the healthcare provided, and found client-centered counseling helpful for adherence. Barriers to adherence included changes in routine, side effects, and stress. Future interventions should leverage existing routines and foster supportive relationships to enhance adherence. A 2012 study by Krakower et al. assessed PrEP awareness and interest among MSM using an internet social networking site. Awareness of PrEP was limited both before and after the release of iPrEx results (13% vs. 19%), though interest remained high (76% vs. 79%). Utilization was low, and further studies are needed to understand barriers to PrEP use among at-risk MSM. A 2012 study in Toronto found high willingness to consider PrEP among MSM undergoing HIV testing, particularly those engaging in high-risk activities. This suggests opportunities for future PrEP use in this population. A 2012 French study assessed interest in an on-demand PrEP trial among MSM. Of 443 HIV-negative respondents, 40% expressed interest in participating. Confidentiality and tailored counseling during follow-up were identified as important considerations. A 2014 study by Mimiaga et al. explored the role of sexual partnerships in PrEP use among high-risk, substance-using MSM. Main partners were seen as supportive of PrEP use, while casual partners presented barriers such as stigma and privacy concerns. Behavioral interventions should be tailored to partner type and relationship dynamics. A 2013 study examined preferences for daily versus intermittent PrEP dosing among substance-dependent, high-risk MSM. Daily dosing was preferred due to ease of integration into routines and concerns about missing doses during substance use. Addressing these preferences may enhance adherence and acceptability. These findings collectively underscore the importance of addressing social, behavioral, and logistical factors in PrEP implementation to improve access and utilization among diverse populations at risk for HIV.
